title: WHY ATHALIAH TRIED TO DESTROY HER OWN FAMILY
paragraphs: WHY ATHALIAH TRIED TO DESTROY HER OWN FAMILY
There are few stories in Scripture as chilling, disturbing, and painfully relevant as the story of Athaliah.
Not because she was a foreign invader.
Not because she led an army.
Not because she was a pagan queen.
But because she tried to destroy her own family.
The tragedy is not merely that Athaliah sought power.
The tragedy is that she was willing to sacrifice the very people she should have protected in order to keep it.
And if we are honest, that story still lives among us.
It appears wherever ambition becomes more important than obedience.
Where control becomes more important than love.
Where legacy becomes more important than faithfulness.
Where people would rather sit on a throne than kneel before God.
The story begins in one of the darkest chapters of Judah's history.
Athaliah was the daughter of King Ahab and Queen Jezebel of Israel (2 Kings 8:18, 26). Through her veins flowed the poisonous influence of two of the most infamous rulers in biblical history.
Ahab's weakness.
Jezebel's rebellion.
Idolatry had become normal.
God's covenant had become secondary.
Power had become everything.
When Athaliah married into the royal family of Judah, she carried that corruption with her.
Scripture repeatedly connects her influence with the spiritual decline of the kingdom.
The biblical writers are careful to show that evil rarely arrives wearing a warning label.
Sometimes it enters through relationships.
Sometimes through compromise.
Sometimes through the gradual acceptance of what God has already condemned.
Then came the moment that changed everything.
Her son, King Ahaziah, died.
Suddenly Athaliah saw an opportunity.
The throne was vulnerable.
The kingdom was unstable.
And instead of trusting God, she chose something far darker.
2 Kings 11:1 records:
"When Athaliah the mother of Ahaziah saw that her son was dead, she arose and destroyed all the royal family."
The Hebrew text uses the verb אָבַד ('avad), carrying the sense of destroying, causing to perish, or exterminating.
This was not a political adjustment.
This was a massacre.
This was calculated annihilation.
She attempted to eliminate every legitimate heir to David's throne.
Every prince.
Every descendant.
Every possible rival.
Every child who stood between her and absolute power.
Think about that for a moment.
These were not foreign enemies.
These were her own grandchildren.
Her own bloodline.
Her own family.
History struggles to comprehend such actions because they seem so unnatural.
Yet Scripture reveals a truth about the human heart that modern culture often refuses to acknowledge.
Sin corrupts absolutely when left unchecked.
The prophet Jeremiah wrote:
"The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick" (Jeremiah 17:9).
Athaliah is what happens when that sickness is allowed to reign.
But there is something even deeper happening beneath the surface.
This story is not merely about political ambition.
It is about spiritual warfare.
God had made a covenant with David.
In 2 Samuel 7, the Lord promised that David's royal line would continue and ultimately produce the Messiah.
The coming Savior would emerge from David's descendants.
Satan understood that promise.
Throughout Scripture we repeatedly see attempts to destroy the messianic line.
Pharaoh ordered Hebrew boys killed.
Haman sought the destruction of the Jews.
Herod slaughtered infants around Bethlehem.
Athaliah's massacre belongs to that same pattern.
If David's line could be extinguished, the promise would appear broken.
The Hebrew word for covenant, בְּרִית (berit), speaks of a binding promise established by God Himself.
And every attack against that covenant ultimately became an attack against God's redemptive plan.
But God was not finished writing the story.
He never is.
Hidden in the darkness was a child.
A baby named Joash.
One surviving heir.
One remaining descendant.
One fragile thread connecting Judah to God's promise.
2 Kings 11:2 tells us that Jehosheba secretly rescued him.
While death moved through the palace halls, she carried life into hiding.
While Athaliah plotted destruction, God was preserving the future.
While evil celebrated victory, heaven was quietly preparing a reversal.
For six years Joash remained hidden.
Imagine the tension.
Imagine the fear.
Imagine the uncertainty.
The kingdom believed David's line was gone.
Athaliah believed she had won.
But God often works where nobody is looking.
The kingdom saw a throne.
God saw a child.
The kingdom saw an ending.
God saw a beginning.
Then came the day everything changed.
The priest Jehoiada revealed Joash publicly.
The rightful king stood before the nation.
The covenant line was alive.
The promise had survived.
Athaliah's response is unforgettable.
She cried:
"קֶשֶׁר קֶשֶׁר"
Qesher! Qesher!
"Treason! Treason!" (2 Kings 11:14)
The irony is staggering.
The woman who stole the throne accused others of conspiracy.
The woman who murdered heirs claimed injustice.
Sin often blinds people to their own hypocrisy.
But truth eventually emerges.
It always does.
Athaliah's reign ended.
God's covenant endured.
David's line survived.
And centuries later another descendant of David entered the world.
Not in a palace.
Not surrounded by armies.
But lying in a manger.
His name was Jesus.
The New Testament opens by carefully tracing His genealogy back to David because the promises had survived every attack.
Every assassination attempt.
Every conspiracy.
Every betrayal.
Every dark chapter.
Including Athaliah.
The Greek word used repeatedly concerning Jesus is Χριστός (Christos), meaning "Anointed One."
He was the fulfillment of every covenant promise.
The King Athaliah could never stop.
The Messiah Satan could never destroy.
The Savior death itself could not hold.
And this is where the story becomes deeply personal.
Most of us will never sit on a throne.
Most of us will never command a kingdom.
But every one of us faces the temptation to place something above God.
Control.
Recognition.
Success.
Influence.
Approval.
Comfort.
The human heart constantly manufactures little thrones.
Athaliah's story warns us what happens when we worship power instead of the One who possesses all power.
Yet the greater message is not her wickedness.
The greater message is God's faithfulness.
Athaliah tried to erase a family.
God preserved a future.
Athaliah tried to destroy a bloodline.
God protected a promise.
Athaliah tried to rewrite history.
Jesus rewrote eternity.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
The Gospel does not begin with good people becoming better.
The Gospel begins with God rescuing people who cannot rescue themselves.
The Apostle Paul wrote that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
Grace arrives where destruction should have won.
Mercy appears where judgment would be deserved.
Hope survives where everything appears lost.
That is why our theme remains so powerful:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe your family history feels broken.
Maybe betrayal has touched your story.
Maybe generations before you made choices that still leave scars.
Maybe you feel trapped by failures that seem impossible to overcome.
Athaliah's story reminds us that darkness never gets the final word.
God specializes in preserving what others try to destroy.
He restores what appears lost.
He redeems what appears ruined.
He writes new chapters where people only see endings.
And perhaps that is exactly what someone reading this needs to hear today.
The story is not over.
The King is still on the throne.
The covenant still stands.
The cross still saves.
The tomb is still empty.
And Jesus Christ is still rewriting lives.
Someone scrolling today may desperately need this reminder that grace is greater than scandal and that God is still writing redemption stories.
Conversations around Scripture have a way of reaching hearts long after the screen is turned off.
What part of Athaliah's story challenged you most?
Because one act of obedience today may become part of someone else's salvation story tomorrow.
The throne Athaliah stole is gone, but the King she could never stop still reigns forever.
